div.p: Limited-preemption forms of uniprocessor scheduling provide a practical trade-off between flexibility and system overheads in embedded kernels. This paper considers the limited-preemption scheduling of implicit deadline tasks using the EDF algorithm. Upper bounds for the occurrence of a deadline miss in these task sets are derived, and employed to create several sufficient schedulability tests of increasing complexity and tightness. Exact analysis is then considered, and an algorithm with polynomial-time complexity is developed for situations in which the CPU utilization is bounded to be less than unity. Experimentally, the sufficient tests are shown to have acceptance ratios increasing from ≈ 60% up to ≈ 99%, and the number of evaluated deadlines required for the exact test is reduced by several orders of magnitude over previously known techniques.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: When viewed purely from the perspective of real-time schedulability analysis, the use of arbitrary task preemptions in uniprocessor real-time systems generally has many benefits. Preemptive systems are generally able to allow higher CPU utilizations -whilst ensuring that deadlines are respected -than non-preemptive systems [1][3] [14]. However when viewed from a slightly wider perspective -which includes factors such as kernel overheads (CPU, memory), resource access protocol requirements and other practical costs of an embedded system implementation, the appeal of non-preemptive schedulers increases significantly [2][3][4][5][6]. Recently, limited-preemption forms of uniprocessor scheduling have been proposed as a practical trade-off between the flexibility of fully preemptive systems with the low resource requirements of their non-preemptive counterparts, and have been found to be a good match for many practical embedded kernels [3][4] [10] [11]. Previous works have considered several different types of limited preemption scheduling, including the general 'floating non-preemptive region' (f-NPR) model which performs well in most aspects, and also encompasses fully non-preemptive scheduling [4]. Both fixed priority and dynamic priority (Earliest Deadline First or EDF) scheduling algorithms have been investigated, see e.g. [3][4] [10] [11]. Investigations of the limited-preemption form of EDF scheduling (lpEDF) have principally considered systems in which one or more tasks has a constrained deadline, and schedulability analysis algorithms for these situations have been developed [3] [10]. The algorithms display pseudo-polynomial runtime complexity when the system utilization is bounded by a fixed constant less than unity, and exponential complexity otherwise.

The fully preemptive scheduling of implicit-deadline or LL tasks -i.e. systems of tasks whose relative deadlines are all equal to their periods [7] -on uniprocessors has been one of the most widely studied areas of real-time computing. Scheduling of these task systems was first investigated by Liu & Layland, who proved the now famous results that the EDF algorithm is optimal in this situation, and that all deadlines will be met by the preemptive earliest-deadline (EDF) algorithm if and only if the system utilization U is less than or equal to unity. On the other hand, for limited and nonpreemptive forms of scheduling there has been comparatively less interest. Uniprocessor scheduling of LL task systems with fully non-preemptive EDF (npEDF) was considered in several previous works, including those of Jeffay et al. [6], Mok & Poon [14] and Jerjukar & Gupta [5]. npEDF was shown to be an optimal nonidling uniprocessor scheduling algorithm for LL tasks, and seems to be well-suited to power aware scheduling applications. Several other works (e.g. [8][9] [15]) have also considered the more general npEDF case of task sets with no presumed relationship between task periods and deadlines, and LL task scheduling on multiprocessor platforms. For LL task systems, although easily computable sufficient conditions for uniprocessor scheduling have been developed (e.g. Corollary 17 in [14] and Theorem 5 in [17]), efforts to date have thus far failed to find an easily computable necessary and sufficient condition for npEDF schedulability which can be evaluated in polynomial time. The best known algorithms to date have pseudo-polynomial complexity.

In this paper the focus is on the uniprocessor lpEDF scheduling of implicit deadline task systems. Despite the optimality of EDF in its various forms, the complexity of uniprocessor EDF schedulability analysis is now known to be weakly coNP-hard in the general case when one or more of the tasks has a deadline less than its period [12]. However the utilization bound for EDF proved by LL in [7] is essentially a special case, in that when all deadlines are equal to (or greater than [9]) their respective periods the schedulability problem can be decided in time linear in the number of tasks. Although results of previous work on limited and non-preemption schedulability analysis of constrained deadline systems generalize to the implicit deadline case, the number of deadlines to be checked becomes proportional to the largest period and is hence pseudo-polynomial. As such, one of the main motivations of this paper is to explore the possibility that a similar relationship between complexity and the nature of the task relative deadlines may be seen in the limited preemption case, i.e. that exact schedulability analysis is 'easier' to perform when deadlines are implicit. The main result of the paper is a confirmation that this result does in fact hold, although the situation is slightly more complex.

A secondary motivation for the current paper is that although most embedded and real-time system developers are familiar with the easily computable EDF utilization bound test of LL, generally speaking they have much less familiarity with the requirements for schedulability analysis of tasks under non-preemptive or limitedpreemptive EDF [13]. The paper also derives some simple sufficient conditions that are syntactically very similar to the regular EDF schedulability condition, and capture the penalty for limited preemption in an easily computable relationship.

The remained of this paper is organized as follows. The assumed system model and additional assumptions are given in Section 2. In Section 3, two bounds on the occurrence of a deadline miss for LL tasks under lpEDF will be developed, and employed to create several sufficient conditions for schedulability of increasing tightness and complexity. An exact schedulability analysis -a limited-preemptive version of the QPA algorithm described in [17] -is presented in Section 4. This Section also contains arguably the main result of the paper, which is a proof that in the worst-case a number of deadlines given by a linear function of the number of tasks need to be checked when the utilization is bounded by a fixed constant less than unity. Section 5 presents the results of a short computation study to investigate the effectiveness of the sufficient conditions developed in Section 3, and to illustrate the performance improvement of the exact algorithm in conjunction with the new bounds. Conclusions are drawn in Section 6.

div.p: The uniprocessor task system to be implemented will be represented by a set T of n recurring (periodic/sporadic) tasks, where each task τ i ∈ T is represented by a three parameter model:

The latter parameter is required since when preemption is not allowed or is limited, the effects of worst-case blocking must be taken into account in the schedulability analysis. Time will be assumed to be discrete, and as such the task parameters can be restricted to be integer and will normally satisfy the relationship 0 ≤ q i < c i < p i . In a fully non-preemptive system each q i will then be equal to c i -1 (see [6], [8] or [9] for justification). Given the restriction to LL task systems it is assumed that the task (relative) deadlines are all equal to periods. Successive arrivals of sporadic tasks are always separated by at least p i units of time, and periodic tasks are always separated by exactly p i time units. The blocking function represents work unavoidable because of limited-preemption which is not included in the demand h(t), and takes on its maximum possible value at t = 0. The paper will also use the following definitions: q max represents the worst-case blocking due to limitedpreemption that may occur in the task set for all values of t > 0, i.e. q max = max 1≤j≤n {q j }. For convenience, let p max = max 1≤j≤n {p j } and let p min = min 1≤j≤n {p j }. It is thought that the penalties for non-preemption can disappear in socalled 'liquid' task sets, i.e. task sets which satisfy the condition q max ≤ ρ x p min for some value of the 'fluidity factor' ρ, where ρ ≤ 1 [15]. In this paper, it will be assumed that ρ is computed as the following ratio:
div.formula: min max p q = ρ (7)
div.p: On a uniprocessor platform, it is a trivial observation that a task set must have a fluidity factor ρ that is strictly less than or equal to unity to ensure schedulability, and ρ ≤ 1 is henceforth implicitly assumed. In order to see why this is necessary condition, consider the arrival of the task with the smallest period τ min arriving at the same instant of time that the maximum blocking begins. Since q max ≥ p min when ρ ≥ 1, no CPU time can be allocated to the job generated by τ min before its deadline, and hence this deadline must be missed.

div.p: As mentioned, although results of previous work on limited and non-preemption schedulability analysis of constrained deadline systems generalize to the implicit deadline case, the number of deadlines to be checked becomes proportional to the largest task period. The bounds thus represent upper limits on the schedulability testing interval -see [8][9] [10] for details. This Section will then employ the bounds to formulate two very simple sufficient conditions that are syntactically very similar to the regular EDF schedulability condition for LL tasks. The graph shows t increasing along the x-axis, and hb(t) increasing along the y-axis, with the boundary line of hb(t) = t starting at the origin and drawn with a slope of 1. The slope of the line projected from q max on the y-axis, through the boundary line at t = p min , gives a limit on the slope of the actual utilization line U to satisfy the sufficient condition. This simple sufficient test places an easily computable bound on the allowable CPU utilization, and is syntactically very similarity to the exact condition for preemptive LL tasks originally derived in [7], with the exception that the 'penalty for non-preemption' is captured as a reduction in the schedulable utilization, depending on the fluidity factor ρ. This loss of schedulable utilization depending on ρ is similar to that found by Baruah in the multiprocessor context [15].

When q max = 0 and no blocking can occur -this happens if we have a fully preemptive system, or with socalled quantum task sets [16] in a fully non-preemptive system (with all tasks having unit execution times)expression (12) reduces to the well-known schedulability condition of preemptive EDF that U ≤ 1. On the other hand, when q max = p min this violates the necessary condition on a uniprocessor, and there is no schedulable utilization whatsoever. Although (12) is pessimistic, it can provide a useful 'rule of thumb' guide to developers of real-time systems as to the likely effects of designing a system using limited-preemptive techniques, and the fluidity factor ρ can be thought of as the 'penalty for limited-preemption' that is paid in terms of the loss in achievable CPU utilization.

div.p: As mentioned, liquid task sets may arise when implementing certain types of real-time system, and in these circumstances it is useful to consider the achievable CPU utilization of lpEDF. For example, if the largest execution time for a fully non-preemptive system can be bounded to be less than a quarter of the smallest period, the schedulable utilization becomes 75%. Since this is higher than the LL bound of 69% for fixed-priority scheduling [7], with no additional mechanisms required for handling shared resources or context switching, such a solution could present a very attractive option for designers of embedded systems with resource constraints.

Equation ( 12) is pessimistic in the sense that it assumes the worst-case blocking exists throughout the entire interval (0, p max ). A trivial observation of tasks under regular EDF is that the task with the shortest relative deadline, once selected for execution, is never preempted [10]. As such, it cannot contribute to the blocking term and can effectively be neglected from the computation of q max . Another observation of equations ( 3) and ( 4) is that the task(s) with the greatest period cannot have both its release time and deadline contained in the interval (0, p max ), and hence cannot contribute to h. These two observations may be extended to tighten the upper bound of (8), by employing an analysis technique similar to that utilized by Jeffay et al. [6] in which the worst-case blocking effects of each task are analyzed in turn, resulting in the bound below.

div.head: Exact Schedulability Analysis
div.p: It was recently shown in a paper by Zhang and Burns [19] that a simple observation regarding the nature of the DBF in a fully preemptive system may be exploited to significantly reduce the average-case number of deadlines to be checked when performing an exact EDF schedulability analysis. In order to carry out an exact schedulability analysis for LL task systems with lpEDF, a limited-preemptive version of the Quick convergence Processor demand Analysis (QPA) algorithm presented in [19] will be developed for LL tasks (the lpQPA-LL algorithm). Starting from the largest required value of t using the bound given by ( 15), lpQPA-LL iterates in a backwards direction until t < p min at which point the search terminates. During this process, a number of redundant deadline checks will be omitted, and schedulability will still be decided exactly. Prior to giving this algorithm, the following Lemma's will be stated, and proof sketches outlined: Lemma 3: The processor demand blocking function hb(t) is monotone non-decreasing in t.

Proof Sketch: We have that h(t) is a monotone nondecreasing function [19]. We also have that b(t) can only change negatively at points of time corresponding to task relative deadlines. Clearly what is 'taken away' from the blocking term when crossing a relative deadline must be added to the processor demand, therefore the summed contribution of the terms hb(t) must be monotone nondecreasing .

Lemma 4: In any task system (either schedulable or unschedulable) with U ≤ 1, if hb(t) ≤ t for some t > 0, then no deadlines are missed by the schedule produced by a limited preemption EDF scheduler in the interval [hb(t), t].

Proof Sketch: Given that U ≤ 1, we have (e.g. from [10]) that a deadline occurring at any particular time t will be missed in the schedule produced by lpEDF if and only if hb(t) > t. Suppose we have a t* such that hb(t*) ≤ t*. We can steadily reduce t from t* until t = hb(t*), and since we have that hb(t) is monotone non-decreasing in t, hb(hb((t*)) cannot be any larger than hb(t*). Thus we can assert that no deadline miss can occur in the interval [hb(t), t].

With these results established, the QPA algorithm as described by [19] may be easily adapted for use in the limited-preemption case, where hb(t) replaces h(t) in most of the steps. The algorithm is given below. Note that an uppercase D is used to represent absolute deadlines of task instances, to distinguish from task relative deadlines.
div.formula: 00 Algorithm 1: lpQPA-LL 01 { 02 if((U>1.0)OR(ρ>1.0)) 03 return(NOT_SCHEDULABLE) 04 t ← max{D i |D i ≤t''} 05 D s ← min{D i |D i >0} 06 while(t ≥ D s ) 07 { 08 if(hb(t)>t)return(NOT_SCHEDULABLE) 09 else t ← max{D i |D i <hb(t)} 10 } 11 return(SCHEDULABLE) 12 }
div.p: The correctness of the lpQPA-LL algorithm follows from Theorem 1 in [19] and the Lemma's stated above. Note that -with appropriate modifications -the algorithm may also be adapted for analysis of constrained deadline task systems. In [19], it was observed that t steadily moves towards 0 in the original QPA algorithm, starting from the initial upper bound. Although many redundant deadlines are skipped, the effect is gradually subdued as U approaches 1. Experimentally, this behavior will again be confirmed for the limited preemption case in the next Section. In terms of worst-case run-time, the upper bound for lpQPA-LL is the value of t'' as computed by (15), and this is clearly proportional to p max in situations when U = 1. Although this bounds the number of deadlines to be checked as a pseudo-polynomial function of the task parameters, when U < 1, the algorithm exhibits significantly better performance; the maximum number of deadlines to be checked is a linear function of n. This is shown in the following Theorem. Theorem 3. When U is bounded from above by some constant 0 < c < 1 such that U ≤ c, lpEDF schedulability analysis of limited preemption task systems using the npQPA-LL algorithm can be performed in polynomial time for each fixed value of c.

Proof: An upper bound on the occurrence of a deadline miss, L, can be calculated using (8) since t'' ≤ t'. When U ≤ c for some fixed constant c, the quantity 1/1-c is also a fixed constant C and we can write:

Therefore an upper bound d' on the maximum number of absolute deadlines any task may have in the testing interval L is given by:
div.formula: C q q C q L d = = = max max max ' (22)
div.p: Which is again a fixed constant; the maximum number of absolute deadlines n tasks may have in the interval L is therefore upper bounded by nC = O(n) for a fixed constant C. The function hb(t) can be computed in time proportional to n for each deadline that requires checking, and we can express the run-time in the asymptotic limit as O(n 2 ) which is polynomial time for any fixed value of 1 > c > 0.

This result shows that in almost every practical situation, lpEDF schedulability analysis can be performed in polynomial time and will be very efficient even when the tasks have large periods. For example when the utilization bound is 0.99 the worst-case number of deadlines to check becomes 100n. In some cases, this constant may be acceptable for use in on-line situations, for example to reduce the computational burden of power-aware scheduling algorithms based around npEDF [5]. As such, it would seem that when attention is restricted to LL tasks the complexity of schedulability analysis in the limited preemption case is reduced over that of the general case. However there are still situations (when U = 1) in which the analysis will take pseudopolynomial time. Given the similarity of the problem to known NP-hard EDF scheduling problems (and the variants of the Directed Diophantine Approximation problem [12]), this seems to indicate that it is weakly coNP-Hard although to the current author's knowledge such a result has yet to be formally shown.

div.head: Computational Results
div.p: In this Section, some simple computational experiments on randomly generated task sets will be used to explore the tightness of the sufficient conditions developed in Section 3 and the performance of the exact algorithm outlined in the previous Section. For the latter, the experiments will attempt to explore the extent to which the new upper bounds and backward iteration technique of lpQPA-LL improve the performance over previous methods. Prior to describing the results, the task parameter generation policy and nature of the experiments will be described.

div.head: Task Parameter Generation / Experiment Design
div.p: The UUnifast algorithm (described in [20]) was employed to uniformly generate the individual task utilizations u i for each task, and computation times c i were uniformly selected from the interval [10,1000] with the period p i computed using p i = c i /u i . In each case, q i was set to c i -1 as this represents the worst-case behavior in terms of schedulability and the length of the required testing intervals. A total of four experiments were carried out, each of which is described below. In the first experiment, task sets were generated and filtered until 10 6 task sets satisfying the necessary condition ρ ≤ 1 had been obtained. Following this, the number of task sets accepted and rejected by three of the tests in Section 3 was compared with the results of the exact schedulability test lpQPA, to give a measure of their acceptance ratios. The three tests considered were ST1 defined by (12), ST2 defined by (19) with both k = 2 and k = 3. In addition, for comparative purposes the test DEVI as described by (18) and the test MOK (as given in [14] and defined by (23)) were also used. The MOK test has complexity O(n) and asserts that a task set verifying the following condition will always meet its deadlines: 0 . 1
div.formula: 1 max ≤ + ∑ = n i i i p q c (23)
div.p: In the second, third and fourth experiments, the average case and worst-case number of iterations (checked deadlines) was recorded as the number of tasks was set at n = 10, n = 20 and n = 30 whilst the processor utilization was varied between U = 0.1 to U = 0.999 in steps of 0.11 for each value of n. In the second experiment, for each configuration of n and U values, task sets were generated and filtered until 10 3 task sets satisfying the necessary condition ρ ≤ 1 had been obtained. For each task set, deadlines were checked in the interval (0, p max ) using forwards iteration until either a deadline was missed, or the tasks deemed schedulable. An identical procedure was employed in the third experiment, with the exception that the bound t'' was employed to replace p max . In the fourth and final experiment, backwards iteration using the bound t'' and the lpQPA-LL algorithm was employed.

div.head: Results and Observations
div.p: For experiment one, the results obtained are as shown in Table I. For experiments two, three and four, the results are plotted graphically in Figs. 234. Note that the numbers of iterations are recorded on logarithmic scales. The acceptance ratio of the proposed tests ST1 was found to be 59.91%, which provides a significant improvement over the test MOK which had an acceptance ratio of only 21.44%. The DEVI test provides a significant improvement over both these tests, increasing the acceptance ratio to 97.64%. As this test is a special case of the proposed ST2 test (i.e. with k = 1), as may be expected increasing k yields successively tighter ratios, with 99.56% for k = 2 and 99.73 for k = 3. However, for increasing k the improvement seems to rapidly diminish, and in addition the average case run-time complexity soon starts to exceed that of the exact lpQPA test.

Considering now Figs. 2 and3, the performance improvement of the new bound t'' can clearly be seen; the maximum number of deadlines checked is reduced from 4,664,332 to 3,665, a reduction factor of 1273. Similarly, the average number of deadlines checked is reduced from 2044 to 22, a reduction factor of 94. Fig. 4 shows a similar dependence on U, and reveals the performance improvement observed by performing backwards iteration. The maximum number of deadlines checked in this case is now reduced to 22, a further reduction factor of 10; the average number of deadlines checked is now reduced to 2, giving a reduction factor which is again very close to 10. Thus whilst the use of backwards iteration gives an additional performance improvement (in most cases, only 2 iterations are required to decide the problem exactly), the improvement is not as pronounced as that to be gained by also adopting the new bound. In addition, it must be observed that for unschedulable task sets, improvements through the use of backwards iteration are not likely to be seen, and the number of iterations may in fact increase in these situations [19].

The results obtained would seem to indicate that the most efficient approaches to decide schedulability for increasing complexity metrics would be to compute test ST2, followed by ST2 with k = 1 then k =2, and finally execute the lpQPA-LL algorithm. Adopting ST2 with k > 2 seems unnecessary as it seems outperformed by lpQPA-LL in almost every situation, despite the theoretical increase in time complexity from O(n log n) to O(n 2 ). A final related observation of interest over all experiments was that on average, 92.7% of task sets satisfying the necessary condition ρ ≤ 1 were actually found to be schedulable in these experiments, which -coupled with the acceptance ratio of the bound ST1 -give an indication of the influence of this parameter on schedulability.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper has considered the limited preemption scheduling of implicit deadline task sets with EDF. The paper has developed several easily computable sufficient tests of increasing complexity, which can be used for online and off-line schedulability analysis. An exact schedulability algorithm (with quadratic complexity when U < 1 and pseudo-polynomial otherwise) has also been presented. The initial computational results reported in the paper show promising performance and improvements over previous techniques.
